A101.text:
La cólera social crece en Francia. La movilización más larga del sector privado y el público en el país marchó en plena huelga por el costo de vida. Al menos en París y en muchas otras ciudades se lanzaron a las calles para combatir un alza del costo de vida insoportable, con un 60 por ciento de inflación alimentaria y salarios que no alcanzan para ir al supermercado ni a la estación de servicio.
Todos están furiosos: desde los policías, que trabajan sin francos, los funcionarios del Estado, los trabajadores del sector privado, los estudiantes, los obreros y el personal sanitario. Todos juntos reclaman aumentos de salarios en un gobierno con sus cajas agotadas. Según la CGT, 500.000 manifestantes en todo el país y para la policía 146.000 marcharon este martes. Para la prefectura hubo 28.000 manifestantes en París.
En la plaza de la Nación, el centro de la partida de la marcha, la secretaria general de la CGT, Sophie Binet, dijo que “solo la respuesta a las reivindicaciones detendrá la movilización. Nada nos detendrá”. Es decir, un aumento de salarios acorde al alza del nuevo costo de vida, un producto de la guerra en Irán y el alza del petróleo.
Menos del 3% (2,59%) de los funcionarios de la administración pública estatal respondieron el martes a la convocatoria de huelga en el sector público, en el marco de una jornada de movilización por los salarios, según una estimación parcial facilitada por el Ministerio de Acción y Cuentas Públicas.
A modo de comparación, cerca del 10% de los empleados públicos de este sector apoyaron la huelga el 5 de noviembre. La administración pública estatal engloba, entre otros, a los trabajadores de los ministerios, las prefecturas y las rectorías, lo que suma un total de unos 2,5 millones de empleados.
El 3,93% de los trabajadores de la sanidad pública estaban en huelga el martes -la misma cifra que el 5 de noviembre-, mientras que en la administración territorial el porcentaje fue del 1,96%, una cifra inferior a la registrada el 5 de noviembre (4,60%).
Vándalos y "Black blocs" al anochecer
Cuando comenzó a bajar la luz a las seis de la tarde en París, los sindicatos abandonaron la plaza de Italia, el final de la concentración, donde casi solo quedaron jóvenes. La mayoría se concentró cerca del centro comercial Italie 2, que se blindó para la ocasión. Al anochecer comienzan los peligros y la violencia.
En París, los policías anunciaron que se disponían a "restablecer la circulación de forma inminente" en la plaza de Italia, instando a los manifestantes que aún permanecían allí a "volver a las veredas". Un centenar de jóvenes se dirigió entonces a toda prisa hacia la entrada del metro, entre cánticos hostiles contra las fuerzas del orden.
"¡Vamos todos a la Bastilla!", gritó uno de ellos. La plaza de la Bastilla estaba blindada por las fuerzas de seguridad y los motociclistas policiales de a dos por moto. Un concierto de sirenas aturde el vecindario.
El temor de los sindicatos es que los Black Blocs anarquistas y los “casseurs” o saqueadores avanzaran y les arruinaran una movilización en calma. Los Black Blocs buscan enfrentarse con la policía y los otros roban el shopping center y sus negocios en las cercanías de la plaza.
Lison, de 20 años y estudiante de una escuela de ingeniería, celebró una manifestación "que ha transcurrido sin violencia y en un ambiente de buena sintonía". También se alegra de haber podido ver a su "ídolo", el líder de izquierda Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a quien no había logrado ver en las movilizaciones anteriores.
Concentración en colegios y universidades
La Justicia suspendió el martes la decisión de la Prefectura de Policía de París de prohibir cualquier concentración o manifestación no declarada, "en un radio de 100 metros", alrededor de diez institutos de enseñanza secundaria y cinco centros universitarios de la capital, según un extracto de la resolución judicial.

A11.text:
‘We want to go back’: Rohingya refugees pin hopes on ICJ genocide verdict
After almost a decade in exile, they're hoping the ICJ rules in their favour. But will that help them get back home?
Cox’s Bazar/Dhaka, Bangladesh — When Dil Hossain and his wife, Alinnesa, fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State during the military crackdown on their Rohingya community in 2017, they carried their newborn daughter, Ishara, and ran for their lives.
Dil’s elderly parents could not escape and were killed as the family fled, along with several other relatives.
“We ran for our lives through mud, hills and water, with the baby tied to us,” Alinnesa recalls.
Nearly nine years later, Ishara is growing up in a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, far from the village where she was born. She has spent almost her entire life in exile. Her parents depend on humanitarian aid, which has declined sharply in recent years, and continue to wait for a chance to return home.
Now, the family is hoping the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will recognise the atrocities committed against the Rohingya. On Thursday, the highest court of the United Nations is due to deliver its judgement in a landmark genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar.
The Gambia filed the case on November 11, 2019, alleging that Myanmar had violated the 1948 Genocide Convention through acts committed against the Rohingya by its military and other security forces.
The allegations concern the so-called “clearance operations” that began in 2016 and escalated in August 2017, which The Gambia says involved genocidal acts intended to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part. The case asks the ICJ to determine Myanmar’s responsibility as a state under the convention.
“The court will find the truth. We suffered, so we know,” Dil said, expressing confidence that the judges would recognise the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.
More than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh, most of them in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Many hope a ruling in their favour will bring recognition of their suffering and strengthen their claim to return home.
But even a landmark legal judgement in their favour may do little to change their lives immediately. Myanmar remains engulfed in civil war, with the same military that committed crimes against the Rohingya still in power, so the prospects for a safe return remain remote.
A life of ’24 hours of depression’ in exile
For many Rohingya refugees, nearly nine years in Bangladesh have brought a different kind of hardship: dependence on aid, uncertainty and a life far removed from the homes they left behind.
Nurul Amin, 25, who works with humanitarian groups in the camps, said the contrast between his former life in Myanmar and his present circumstances was stark.
“Back home, we had houses, big trees, gardens and farmland. We could grow our own food and did not have to depend on others. We were self-sufficient,” he said. “Here, we have to depend on others for almost everything. The difference is like that between heaven and earth.”
Years of displacement have also taken a toll on his mental wellbeing, he said. “It is 24 hours of depression. It feels as though we have lost our world, as though the world has abandoned us.”
Mohammad Rehan, now 18, was a child when the military crackdown began, but retains vivid memories that he says have left a lifelong mark.
“The most horrific thing I saw was houses being burned. It made me really afraid,” he said. “I was very young at the time, and those scenes left me traumatised.”
He hopes the court will recognise the Rohingya’s suffering and their right to equal treatment.
“If they find Myanmar guilty, I think it will help our community return and reclaim our rights,” he said.
What justice means for the Rohingya
The case brought by The Gambia accuses Myanmar of violating its obligations under the convention through the military’s treatment of the Rohingya, particularly during the 2017 crackdown.

A111.text:
Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party, with 66 voting in favor of Kahana and 52 voting for another candidate, according to the office of the spokesperson for the parliament.
Kahana replaces Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party.
"The Knesset of Israel is the home of all citizens of the State of Israel, and I intend to be the Speaker for everyone," said Kahana in his inaugural speech.
In Israel's unicameral 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, the speakership is a powerful position that wields considerable influence, including over what legislation is brought to a vote.
Kahana will have the ability to advance bills prioritised by the Eisenkot-led bloc and other parties backing the former general in his bid to become prime minister.
These include establishing an independent inquiry into the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, which Netanyahu has opposed; imposing term limits on the prime minister; and repealing laws passed by the previous Netanyahu-led government that critics said curtailed the powers of the judiciary.
Netanyahu's Likud party condemned the vote, saying lawmakers elected Kahana with "the votes of terror supporters." Throughout the election campaign, Netanyahu attacked Israel's Arab-led parties saying that they represent an existential threat to Israel, in attacks that the parties condemned as racist and discriminatory.
Members of the Eisenkot-led bloc have also been appointed to chair several key parliamentary committees, which play an important role in advancing legislation.
The parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after a deadlocked October 27 general election stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left his main rivals with no clear path to power.
DEADLOCKED ELECTION AFTERMATH
President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar political party, with forming a government. However, the former chief of the military also lacks a majority and will likely have to compromise on some campaign promises if he is to secure the support needed to form a government.
Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a government is formed. His right-wing Likud's alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats.
Eisenkot's Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel's Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
Netanyahu has sought to cast doubt on the election results by baselessly alleging voter fraud by Arabs, who make up a fifth of the population. Election officials have said that they are probing potential misconduct but that they have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the vote's outcome.
Israel's Channel 12 News reported on Sunday that law enforcement was investigating whether officials in Netanyahu's office had deliberately planted information that prompted an inquiry into alleged vote-buying in Arab communities.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the Channel 12 report as "false".
(Reporting by Alexander Cornwell, Editing by Hugh Lawson and Sanjeev Miglani)

A146.text:
Frontferne Ziele USA kritisieren ukrainische Angriffe im Inneren Russlands
Die USA haben nach dem jüngsten ukrainischen Angriff auf die Krimbrücke deutliche Kritik an der Zielauswahl der ukrainischen Militärführung geübt.
Die öffentliche Debatte konzentriere sich auf das »auf die spektakulären Angriffe weit hinter den Frontlinien«, die der russischen Bevölkerung Leid zufügen sollten, sagte Verteidigungsstaatssekretär Elbridge Colby bei einem Treffen von Verbündeten der Ukraine im Nato-Hauptquartier in Brüssel.
Dabei komme die USA »zu der Einschätzung, dass solche Angriffe weder dazu beigetragen haben, ein Ende des Krieges herbeizuführen, noch dazu, den russischen Vormarsch an der Front aufzuhalten«, sagte der US-Vertreter.
Darüber hinaus stärkten solche Angriffe wahrscheinlich sogar die Entschlossenheit der russischen Bevölkerung und die Bereitschaft des Kreml zur Eskalation. Dies gelte insbesondere für Angriffe, die sich gegen zivile Infrastruktur wie die des Online-Riesen Wildberries richteten, fügte Colby hinzu und wies dabei auch auf Russlands Fähigkeiten zu Vergeltungsschlägen im ukrainischen Hinterland hin.
Den ukrainischen Angriff auf die für Russland strategisch wichtige Brücke auf die Halbinsel Krim erwähnte Colby nicht explizit. Nach Angaben von Diplomaten dürften die Äußerungen des US-Staatssekretärs für Verteidigungspolitik allerdings mit diesem in direktem Zusammenhang stehen.
Rutte hält Schlag gegen Krimbrücke für legitim
Zuvor hatten europäische Politiker den ukrainischen Angriff auf die von Russland erbaute Brücke zur Halbinsel Krim als legitimes und notwendiges Verteidigungsmanöver gewertet.
Es sei »ziemlich dumm«, Angriffe zur Zerstörung militärischer Ziele in Russland zu kritisieren, sagte Verteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius in Reaktion auf Colby. Man solle eher über die täglichen und nächtlichen »terroristischen Angriffe« auf die zivile Energie-, Wasser- und Wärmeversorgung in der Ukraine sprechen als über legale und legitime Schläge gegen nicht-zivile Ziele in Russland.
Nato-Generalsekretär Mark Rutte unterstützte diese Position, wenn auch mit gemäßigteren Worten. Rutte sagte am Rande des Treffens der Ukraine-Unterstützergruppe, es sei wichtig, dass sich die Ukraine verteidige. Dies bedeute auch, logistische Knotenpunkte anzugreifen.
Ein vom ukrainischen Sicherheitsdienst veröffentlichtes Bild zeigt die zerstörte Krimbrücke
Foto:
Ukrainian Security Service / AFP
Der britische Verteidigungsminister Wes Streeting erklärte: »Ich denke, wir haben gerade ein weiteres Beispiel für den Einfallsreichtum der Ukrainer und die unbedingte Entschlossenheit der Ukraine gesehen, sich gegen die russische Aggression zu verteidigen.« Man stehe der Ukraine dabei zur Seite.
Indirekt forderte Colby die europäischen Verbündeten sogar auf, solche Angriffe nicht zu unterstützen. Die Unterstützung sollte darauf ausgerichtet sein, die Ukraine in die Lage zu versetzen, die Frontlinie zu halten und, wo immer möglich, Geländegewinne zu erzielen. »Angriffe, die sich auf die Frontlinie konzentrieren und die unmittelbare Unterstützung der Kampfhandlungen in diesem Gebiet fallen selbstverständlich in diese Kategorie«, ergänzte er.
Zudem könnten im Einklang mit diesem Ansatz auch Angriffe auf Russlands Kriegsmaschinerie sein, die den russischen Vormarsch an der Front verlangsamen. Die Ukraine sollte nicht gezwungen werden, mit auf dem Rücken gefesselten Händen zu kämpfen, betonte er.
Kyjiw fordert weitere Kampfjets
Die Ukraine verteidigt sich mit westlicher Hilfe seit mehr als viereinhalb Jahren gegen eine groß angelegte russische Invasion. Die Ukraine braucht nach Worten von Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj 40 weitere Kampfjets vom US-Typ F-16. Es sei ein starker Kampfjet, aber er brauche auch viel Wartung, sagte Selenskyj.
Kyjiw beklagt seit Langem einen Mangel an Flugabwehrraketen zum Schutz gegen von Russland eingesetzte ballistische Raketen. US-Systeme vom Typ Patriot gelten als wirksames Mittel zur Abwehr.

A148.text:
Berichte über Präsenz in der Ukraine Russland sieht Kriegsbeteiligung Frankreichs
Nach Berichten über die Präsenz französischer Soldaten in der Ukraine hat der russische Außenminister Sergej Lawrow Frankreich die Teilnahme am Krieg vorgeworfen. »Es geht nicht nur um Franzosen, das wissen wir. Das ist keine Unterstützung der Ukraine mehr, das ist eine direkte Beteiligung am Krieg«, sagte Lawrow in Manila am Rande eines Gipfeltreffens der Vereinigung Südostasiatischer Nationen (Asean).
Laut Berichten des Senders RFI , die unter anderem die Zeitung »Le Monde« bestätigte, befinden sich seit mehreren Monaten französische Soldaten in der Ukraine, um dort ukrainische Soldaten auszubilden und militärisches Gerät zu warten. Die Mission »Volia« wird nach Informationen von RFI von einem französischen General geleitet und hat eine »leichte und anpassungsfähige Struktur«.
Bereits seit 2023 französische Mission in Polen
Der französische Einsatz in der Ukraine nutzt laut RFI eine bereits seit 2023 bestehende Mission in Polen, die ebenfalls der Ausbildung ukrainischer Soldaten dient. Diese Mission, die Teil einer EU-Mission ist, sei das »Eingangstor« der französischen Soldaten zur Ukraine.
Die französische Regierung bestätigt die Präsenz eigener Soldaten in der Ukraine, weist aber den russischen Vorwurf einer direkten Beteiligung im Krieg entschieden zurück. Diese Behauptung sei absurd, die entsandten Soldaten hätten keine Kampfabsicht, sagte die beigeordnete Ministerin im französischen Verteidigungsministerium, Alice Rufo, in der Nationalversammlung.
Rufo sagte, es gebe in der Ukraine eine Koordinierungsstelle, die eng mit der französischen Verteidigungsmission zusammenarbeite. Das ermögliche, punktuell gezielte Schulungen sowie Wartungs- und Instandhaltungsarbeiten durchzuführen. Die Einsätze seien punktuell, die Zahl der eingesetzten Kräfte sei sehr begrenzt, fügte sie hinzu, ohne die Aussage zu konkretisieren. Auf der Plattform X schrieb sie: »Wir sind keine Kriegspartei in der Ukraine.«
Der Einsatz in der Ukraine wird unter anderem mit der Wartung der Rüstungsgüter begründet, die Frankreich an die Ukraine geliefert hat. Dazu zählen Artilleriesysteme vom Typ Caesar und Kampfjets vom Typ Mirage 2000.
Bislang hatte kein westliches Land bestätigt, Soldaten oder Spezialeinheiten in der Ukraine zu haben. Auf russischer Seite beteiligen sich nordkoreanische Soldaten an dem Krieg gegen die Ukraine.
Jahrelang blieben der Ukraine Marschflugkörper verwehrt, die besonders für Schläge auf Brückenpfeiler geeignet sind. Nun hat das Land eine eigene Lösung gefunden. Wie die Ukraine die Kertschbrücke zum Einsturz brachte, lesen Sie hier .

A15.text:
China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
The president says Beijing seeks to provide a ‘stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises’.
China’s President Xi Jinping has urged support for “free and open trade”, pitching Beijing as a stable partner – as opposed to President Donald Trump-led Washington – and pledging to stand up to trade protectionism.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Wednesday in Shenzhen, southern China, Xi took aim at rising “unilateralism and protectionism”.
His remarks appeared to be a veiled criticism of Trump’s America First policies, under which the United States has imposed tariffs on both allies and economic rivals.
Xi is due to meet Trump, who is travelling from the Philippines for the APEC leaders’ summit later on Wednesday. Xi and Trump are then due to hold an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the sidelines of the APEC summit, Xi told business executives that the Asia Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.
Trump’s America First approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone.
Washington also limits Chinese access to leading-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help power artificial intelligence (AI).
“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains,” Xi said.
He added that China sought to “provide a more stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises” and would continue to expand access in its manufacturing and services sectors.
“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access, and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told the Associated Press news agency that Xi’s speech highlighted China’s aim to lead global industrial transformation.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia, or the US directly.
Xi’s message is “likely to resonate with many Global South countries, and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington”, Chen added.

A158.text:
Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
November 17, 2026
During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.
Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
What does Russia mean by 1997?
The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.
According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.
What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?
A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.
In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.
"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."
The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.
Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?
In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.
For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.
Who decides which alliances a country can join?
As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.
[truncated]

A160.text:
Ethiopia-Eritrea border clashes raise fears of regional war
November 17, 2026
After a few weeks of relative stability, fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border areahave raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudanhave hit new lows.
Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23. It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia.
According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme.
While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War.
The war ended with theAlgiers Agreement, in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea, a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles.
"It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said.
He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region.
The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea
"The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time", Abdurahman Sayed said.
Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forcesduring the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties. At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray.
Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces.
"So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW.
However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time."
Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab, by force.
Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads
At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further.
[truncated]

A17.text:
Russia, China should ‘lead’ push to multipolar world, Xi tells APEC summit
Putin says Western powers are ‘former hegemons’, with Europe in the midst of a ‘humiliating decline’.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has said that Beijing and Moscow should “lead and advance the trend towards a multipolar world” following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Xi and Putin held bilateral discussions on Wednesday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Following Xi, Putin took to the stage, telling the summit that Western powers were “former hegemons”, adding that Europe was in the midst of a “humiliating decline”.
“Experience has shown that the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having lost much of their intimidating power,” Putin said.
“While sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth – let alone crushing the economies of competitors.”
Russia’s economy has been heavily sanctioned by the US and Europe because of its war against Ukraine, which began in February 2022 when Moscow invaded its neighbour.
Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Shenzhen, said that both Xi and Putin called for a “more fair and multipolar world order and that the two leaders also said they would maintain close ties amid what they both described as global uncertainty”.
She added that Xi and Putin “have a close personal relationship, and they have met more than 40 times over the years, and these two countries are also strategically aligned”, with China remaining Russia’s biggest trading partner, and Russia providing Beijing with much-needed energy resources.
“Putin clearly took a swing at European countries, in particular, that have put sanctions on Russia,” Yu added.
But in Shenzhen, “Putin is having a bit of a moment in the sun” at the APEC summit, where he is being treated as a guest of honour.
Differing expectations
Robert Kelly, a professor of political science at Pusan National University in South Korea’s Busan, said that all three leaders are “coming in with fairly different expectations and desires of what they want”.
“That’s going to make it quite difficult for them to actually find an agreement,” he said. “Nuclear weapons is an area where the three leaders could really make some great progress,” he argued, adding that the current “tripolar world of nuclear powers is different than the Cold War”.
“It would be great if the three of them could actually bring [the arms race] under control,” Kelly told Al Jazeera.
“But all the different parties are in different places – for the Russians, their weapons are very important to bolster their perception as a great power, despite their problems in Ukraine,” he noted.
“The Chinese have engaged in a major buildup, and it doesn’t look like they want arms control, nuclear weapons at least in their 10 years; and the United States has been sort of very standoffish about any kind of deal,” Kelly said.
“There’s a very strong public goods argument for a positive outcome, for an arms control agreement, but it just won’t happen,” he added.
APEC was established in 1989 and has 21 members, accounting for more than 50 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and representing about 2.7 billion people.
The organisation aims to support economic growth and prosperity in the Asia Pacific region.
Leaders are expected to discuss a range of important issues at this year’s summit, including artificial intelligence (AI) and trade – two areas in which the US and China play dominant roles.
A key issue for APEC members and the wider world is the trade truce between Washington and Beijing, and whether it will be extended beyond January.

A19.text:
Africa’s economic future cannot depend on Washington
Trump’s move to exclude South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA shows why Africa must accelerate its own economic integration.
On September 2 , United States President Donald Trump signed legislation extending the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) through the end of 2028, following overwhelming support in Congress. Yet just two months later, on November 2 , his administration announced plans to terminate the eligibility of South Africa and Rwanda for the programme from January 1, 2027.
The decision lays bare the fundamental weakness of AGOA: African economies depend on trade privileges that Washington can withdraw whenever its political priorities change.
AGOA is a US trade law that currently covers 33 eligible sub-Saharan African countries. It was enacted on May 18, 2000, to allow these countries to export thousands of products to the US market duty-free, and was promoted as a strategic mechanism to foster economic growth, expand trade between the US and the continent and encourage economic and political reforms.
AGOA initially delivered promising results. It is estimated to have supported more than 300,000 direct jobs across Africa and 1.3 million indirect jobs. According to a 2024 US Trade Representative report, two-way goods trade between the US and sub-Saharan Africa reached $47.5bn in 2023, including $9.7bn in imports under AGOA and the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP), of which $5.5bn consisted of non-oil products such as apparel and agricultural goods.
However, recent figures point to growing challenges, with some even suggesting a decline. A Congressional Research Service report shows that US imports receiving AGOA duty-free treatment dropped sharply from $7.9bn in 2024 to $5bn in 2025. Another analysis by the German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) noted that the share of US imports from sub-Saharan Africa benefiting from AGOA and GSP preferences plummeted from more than 80 percent in 2008 to roughly 24.7 percent in 2021 amid eligibility uncertainty and short renewal windows.
Only a few eligible sub-Saharan African countries capture most of the programme’s benefits. South Africa is its largest beneficiary, with exports to the US worth billions of dollars annually, while most other eligible countries struggle to make full use of its preferences.
Furthermore, because the US administers the programme’s preferences unilaterally, rather than through a bilateral treaty, Washington can exclude or reinstate any eligible country based on its own assessments and criteria, including market reforms, human rights and labour standards.
Since the programme’s inception, some countries suspended from AGOA have criticised the impact of their removal. Ethiopia’s suspension in 2022, for instance, led to the loss of thousands of garment sector jobs.
In practice, Washington’s geopolitical interests often carry more weight in eligibility decisions than AGOA’s stated criteria.
The Trump administration’s decision to terminate South Africa’s and Rwanda’s AGOA eligibility is a clear case in point. Both countries have pursued policies that conflict with Washington’s interests and that the administration regards as a threat. South Africa has strengthened its economic and political ties with US rivals such as China and Russia, while facing accusations from Washington of obstructing American trade and investment, alongside Trump’s allegations of a “white genocide”.
Rwanda’s alleged support for the M23 rebel group in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has also brought it into conflict with US interests in the region’s critical minerals.
Sharp declines in AGOA import values, unstable US trade policies, and short-term extensions leave African exporters highly vulnerable. Losing AGOA access triggers immediate customs setbacks, including tariff increases of 15 to 20 percent on some products.

A251.text:
Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.
Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.
The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.
Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.
Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.
A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System
To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.
DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.
And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.
In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers.

A27.text:
Iran fires at Kuwait, widening strikes after US hit Iranian island
By Enas Alashray and Nayera Abdallah
DUBAI, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Iran said it targeted US drone and missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the United States struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking Tehran's first attack on the US-allied Gulf state since September.
Underlining a broader uptick in hostilities in recent days, Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday for a third time in a week, accusing Tehran of a "systematic hostile approach" towards the Gulf kingdom, where the US Navy's Fifth Fleet is headquartered.
The latest attacks highlighted the obstacles facing diplomatic efforts to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices and drawn in countries across the region.
IRAN ISSUES FRESH WARNING TO 'THE ENEMY'
The Iranian army said it had targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base after Kuwait said its air defences were countering hostile drone attacks.
It followed US airstrikes on Tuesday evening, when American fighter aircraft targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm in retaliation for Iranian attacks on US personnel and assets, a US military official told Reuters. Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack caused no damage to infrastructure.
Kuwait said it reserved the right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and protect its territory and vital facilities against any aggression or threat.
In videos published by state media on Wednesday, Iranian Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami issued a fresh warning to the United States, which launched the war against Iran alongside Israel in February.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.
MEDIATOR QATAR AIMS TO NARROW GAPS
The United States and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 and Tehran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases.
The conflict later spread to Lebanon, where fighting erupted between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah, and to Yemen, from where the Iran-aligned Houthis have launched attacks on Saudi energy facilities, airports and other targets.
Global oil and gas prices have shot up with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted after Tehran declared it closed, while the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iran, hitting Iran's economy hard.
Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said.
A Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital Riyadh.
There was no immediate confirmation from the Houthis.
A surge in attacks on shipping since October has threatened to further strain global oil supplies. On Tuesday, a crew abandoned a liquefied petroleum gas tanker off Oman's Khasab.
The United Arab Emirates' ADNOC L&S said on Wednesday that one crew member was missing and 11 injured after one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
RUBIO SEES NO IMMINENT THREAT TO WASHINGTON
Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack on Washington, when asked about a CNN report that cited US intelligence assessments on a potential Iranian plot involving a so-called dirty bomb.
OnWednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital.
Iran's Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them "baseless."
A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to disperse radioactive material.

A28.text:
Gulf nations attacked after US strikes Iranian island
Bahrain and Kuwait said Wednesday that they had repelled air attacks launched against them following US strikes on an Iranian island, as Gulf nations face retaliatory bombardment in the Middle East war.
The conflict -- which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February -- has spilled over to Gulf states that host US military facilities.
The Iranian army said Wednesday its drones "targeted Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms belonging to the terrorist US military at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait," in a statement carried by state television IRIB.
Kuwait's military said Wednesday its air defences were "responding to hostile drone threats", urging its public to follow security and safety advice.
While Bahrain said its air defences intercepted attacks from Iran early Wednesday, a day after Tehran's Revolutionary Guards said they attacked a base used by Washington.
The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close the waterway.
Iran's official IRNA news agency cited a regional official as saying the United States had hit Qeshm Island in the Hormuz strait without causing serious damage.
US fighter jets "used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island", an American official told AFP on condition of anonymity, adding that the strike was in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets".
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Iran-backed group toward the Riyadh area.
- Alleged Iran plot -
Explosions boomed across Bahrain's capital on Tuesday as a mobile phone alert warned residents to seek safety.
Bahrain's armed forces said they "confronted, intercepted and destroyed a number of treacherous Iranian aerial attacks today... before they could achieve their objectives", while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they targeted a US-operated radar system.
"Combat drones belonging to the Revolutionary Guards carried out a precision operation this morning, targeting a radar system operated by US forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the Guards' Sepah news website said.
The attack was in response to the "repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones", it added. The Guards also said they had intercepted and captured a US drone south of Qeshm.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, was heavily targeted earlier in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, but had not been hit for weeks until Iranian drone attacks on Friday and Sunday.
Despite Washington and Tehran holding back from a full resumption of hostilities, the sides have traded fire and accusations.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday he was taking "very seriously" reports that Iran was developing plans to use a so-called "dirty bomb" in Washington.
CNN cited seven anonymous US officials as saying Iran was plotting how to target senior administration figures with a bomb laced with chemical or radioactive material, though they stopped short of saying Iran planned to carry out such an attack.
"If there is (such a threat), they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before," Trump said, adding: "I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy."
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the report and called it "Iraq War-style propaganda".
- 'Fear and anxiety' -
"I was on my way to work when the warning sirens went on," Abdulrahman Abdullah, a Bahraini civil servant in his forties, told AFP on Tuesday.
"Fear and anxiety rise as attacks increase...

A31.text:
Israeli parliament elects speaker backed by Netanyahu opponents
JERUSALEM, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Israel's parliament voted on Tuesday to select a new speaker opposed to the agenda of Benjamin Netanyahu, a potential first step in rolling back theprime minister's divisive political agenda even as his main rival struggles to form a government.
Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party, with 66 voting in favor of Kahana and 52 voting for another candidate, according to the office of the spokesperson for the parliament.
Kahana replaces Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party.
"The Knesset of Israel is the home of all citizens of the State of Israel, and I intend to be the Speaker for everyone," said Kahana in his inaugural speech.
In Israel's unicameral 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, the speakership is a powerful position that wields considerable influence, including over what legislation is brought to a vote.
Kahana will have the ability to advance bills prioritised by the Eisenkot-led bloc and other parties backing the former general in his bid to become prime minister.
These include establishing an independent inquiry into the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, which Netanyahu has opposed; imposing term limits on the prime minister; and repealing laws passed by the previous Netanyahu-led government that critics said curtailed the powers of the judiciary.
Netanyahu's Likud party condemned the vote,sayinglawmakers elected Kahana with "the votes of terror supporters." Throughout the election campaign, Netanyahu attacked Israel's Arab-led parties saying that they represent an existential threat to Israel, in attacks that the parties condemned as racist and discriminatory.
Members of the Eisenkot-led bloc have also been appointed to chair several key parliamentary committees, which play an important role in advancing legislation.
The parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after a deadlocked October 27 general election stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left his main rivals with no clear path to power.
DEADLOCKED ELECTION AFTERMATH
President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar political party, with forming a government. However, the former chief of the military also lacks a majority and will likely have to compromise on some campaign promises if he is to secure the support needed to form a government.
Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a government is formed. His right-wing Likud's alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats.
Eisenkot's Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in theparties representing Israel's Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
Netanyahu has sought to cast doubt on the election results by baselessly alleging voter fraud by Arabs, who make up a fifth of the population. Election officials have said that they are probing potential misconduct but that they have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the vote's outcome.
Israel's Channel 12 News reported on Sunday that law enforcement was investigating whether officials in Netanyahu's office had deliberately planted information that prompted an inquiry into alleged vote-buying in Arab communities.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the Channel 12 report as "false".
(Reporting by Alexander Cornwell, Editing by Hugh Lawson and Sanjeev Miglani)

A32.text:
Israel parliament elects Eisenkot ally as speaker in blow for Netanyahu
Israeli lawmakers on Tuesday elected a parliament speaker from the camp opposed to caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a first step towards rolling back the legacy of the country's divisive veteran leader.
Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.
The parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister who has been in and out of office for three decades.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the 120-member Knesset in October 27 elections, with the two blocs trading barbs since then.
The vote for parliament speaker crystallised their standoff, with a heated debate before the vote.
In October, Eisenkot's wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu's finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu's hard-right government.
On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot's candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.
"I intend to be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender," said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Eisenkot congratulated him on his victory, and wrote on X that "a new chapter begins" while Likud lamented on the same platform "the eternal disgrace" of a Knesset speaker elected thanks to the votes of Arab lawmakers.
Netanyahu's and Eisenkot's parties met Sunday on the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume war on Iran, has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.
Eisenkot said afterwards that Netanyahu was unfit to "remain at the helm of government for even one more minute" after an explosive media report that his allies tried to make up allegations of fraud to frame lawmakers from the Arab minority.
On Tuesday, Israel's central elections committee released a statement regarding the ongoing investigation into the fraud accusations led by the Shin Bet intelligence agency.
"At this stage, there is no evidence that bribes were paid to voters on a scale that could have affected the election results," it said.
- Targeting Netanyahu era -
With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu's legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
The judicial reforms initiated shortly after Netanyahu began his latest term in December 2022 triggered some of Israel's largest ever protests, bringing tens of thousands to the streets, with liberals fearing an erosion of the country's democracy.
Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel's security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.
[truncated]

A35.text:
NSA’s secret communications system suffers hourslong outage: What to know
The disruption comes amid a string of apparently unrelated US service outages this week.
WASHINGTON — The US National Security Agency’s main classified communications system experienced a prolonged disruption on Tuesday without immediate explanation from the agency.
A person familiar with the outage told Al-Monitor that the agency’s NSANet intranet, which handles secret and top-secret internal messaging, had been down from early Tuesday morning through the afternoon after prior interruptions over the past month. CNN first reported the outage, citing six US officials.
The spy agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon that it “experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” and that “some internal systems were affected” but “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational.”
Al-Monitor has reached out to the White House for comment.
The outage at the nation’s top signals intelligence agency marked the latest in a series of apparently random cyber outages in the United States over the past week.
On Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook, one of the world’s largest corporate email providers, suffered a global outage that the company attributed to a "latent defect" related to insufficient server capacity.
On Nov. 13, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a total grounding of all commercial flights in US airspace after a communications disruption at several airports on the East Coast, which US Homeland Security Director Markwayne Mullin blamed on a faulty software upgrade to the nation’s air traffic control communications systems.
Some major financial institutions in the US, including JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, also reported service outages for customers this week. A number of United Airlines flights were also delayed on Monday afternoon for roughly an hour due to what the company called a “widespread system outage,” which it later said was resolved.
The apparently unrelated incidents have drawn speculation about potential cyberattacks against the United States, coming ahead of US President Donald Trump’s scheduled Nov. 19 meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. The string of outages also comes as the Trump administration settles into a holding pattern while the war with Iran remains stalemated.
The person familiar with the intranet outage at the NSA said there was no evidence to suspect a cyberattack at this time. The source also said they had seen no evidence that the outage was planned.

From contract killers to cartels: A history of Iran-linked plots on US soil
A reported Iranian plot to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington has put Tehran’s capacity to strike inside the United States under scrutiny.
WASHINGTON — Reported plans for a possible Iranian “dirty bomb” attack in Washington have raised fresh concerns about Tehran’s ability to strike on US soil.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is “looking into” allegations in a CNN report that Iran is developing plans to target top Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon. The report said there is no indication of an imminent attack but that the “very specific” plotting includes locations and targets.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the outlet that the United States is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
But the Iranian threat to Americans appears to have grown more acute since the start of the war, nearly nine months ago. US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in a declassified memo in October that Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” abroad, with the “lethal plotting efforts” having reached “advanced stages.”

A39.text:
Araghchi meets Qatari mediators in Oman as Trump threatens Iran over dirty bomb report
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with officials from Oman and Qatar as Washington and Tehran exchanged fresh strikes.
WASHINGTON — Regional mediators pushed Tuesday for a deal between the United States and Iran as President Donald Trump said his administration was “looking into” whether Tehran was planning to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with a delegation from Qatar, the main mediator between the warring countries, during a visit to the Omani capital, Muscat, on Tuesday. Majed al-Ansari, a Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman, said the delegation would seek to “narrow differences and reach an agreement to end the war.”
Earlier Tuesday, Araghchi sat down with Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi in Muscat to discuss the Strait of Hormuz and “the importance of safeguarding the security of maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of international shipping and trade,” according to the Omani Foreign Ministry.
Iran has said it would reopen the vital strait within two days if the United States agreed to its demands, which include major sanctions relief, the release of billions of dollars in frozen assets and compensation for war damage. US officials have dismissed many of those conditions as nonstarters.

A4.text:
As Trump arrives in China, low expectations for breakthroughs in rivalry
Analysts expect few concrete outcomes from talks between the leaders on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
For more than a year, the United States and China have maintained an uneasy truce in their intense technological and economic rivalry.
As US President Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday for his third meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping since hitting pause on the US-China trade war last year, expectations for major breakthroughs are low.
At the Shenzhen airport, Xi greeted Trump — Chinese presidents rarely welcome visiting guests when they land — even as journalists travelling with the US president waited on Air Force One.
Yet despite the red carpet welcome, analysts expect few concrete agreements out of Trump and Xi’s meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
Instead, the two leaders are expected to focus on stabilising ties between Washington and Beijing at a time when their differences are in full view amid claims that chip giant Nvidia’s former CEO was targeted in a Chinese espionage operation.
Trump and Xi each benefit from “projecting a sense of having things under control in the US-China relationship,” said Ryan Hass, director of the John L Thornton China Center at Brookings.
“I do not expect that dynamic to change in the coming period,” Hass told Al Jazeera.
“Their ability to continue to guide the relationship will be challenged in the coming year, though, since they will not have as many opportunities for direct leader-level diplomacy as they did in 2026,” he added.
Ahead of the talks, Trump has sought to downplay the controversy surrounding Nvidia, which revolves around former CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Megaspeed executive accused of being a Chinese spy.
The scandal has highlighted tensions within the Trump administration over China’s access to AI chips amid suspicions that Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore, diverted Nvidia GPUs to the country in violation of US export controls.
On Monday, US prosecutors confirmed that it had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed amid recriminations over the US Department of Commerce’s failure to place the firm on its export control list.
“We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Trump, who will also join an unprecedented three-way meeting involving Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at APEC, told reporters on Monday.
Beijing has denied the spying claims, calling them “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”.
Rana Mitter, S T Lee Chair in US-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, said he expected “little mention” of Nvidia in public.
“China denies involvement, and Trump has stated that he doesn’t intend to raise it,” Mitter told Al Jazeera.
“Also, the US administration is still divided on the best course of action,” he said.
“Overall, the Trump administration will look to maintain the current detente, but the underlying competition remains strong.”
Renewed trade war
Trump and Xi have held three face-to-face meetings aimed at lowering the temperature in the US-China rivalry since the US president kicked off a renewed trade war against Beijing upon his return to the White House.
Amid tit-for-tat trade salvoes, tariff rates for Chinese and US goods rose as high as 145 percent and 125 percent, respectively, until Trump and Xi agreed to a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, in October last year.
The truce is currently set to expire on January 10, 2027, after Washington and Beijing agreed to extend the agreement beyond its original expiration date of November 10.
Speaking at the opening of the two-day APEC summit on Wednesday, Xi reiterated Beijing’s opposition to protectionism and unilateralism, urging countries to support “free and open trade and investment” and “inclusive and balanced development”.
