A44.text:
On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”
Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “horrible idea.” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.
Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported.
If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.
Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.
“Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”
Trump officials accused of “corruption”
What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.”
“I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”
Yoon noted that evidencesuggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.
The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported. He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.
[truncated]

A55.text:
Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
- Published
Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."
Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.
The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
- How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? 
  - Published4 hours ago
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
[truncated]

A56.text:
Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
- Published
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.
Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.
In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.
Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.
Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.
Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.
He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.
"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.
Technology-related disruptions have happened almost daily since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.
The next day, the US Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the US for more than four hours with a rare national ground stop. It was the longest halting of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US.
The US transport secretary said the issue was technical and caused by a copper wire upgrade and outdated equipment.
On Monday, a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted service at the biggest and most utilised banks in the US.
Both United and Chase said a software issue was behind the glitch.
Apple users were impacted by outages affecting iCloud and Apple Pay on Tuesday. The company said the cause was not a cyber-attack but the outage was triggered by an an internal update.
The same day, a highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications also went offline for a period of time.
Tech experts weigh in: 'No conspiracy here'
Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.
Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages.
"There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC.
"There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."
Beevers said AI is only part of the story.
"It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said.
[truncated]

A58.text:
Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
- Published
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
[truncated]

A60.text:
'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
- Published
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.
The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.
A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.
The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.
Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.
The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"What else could I do?" she shrugged.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

A606.text:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
[truncated]

A68.text:
Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
- Published
President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."
CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.
Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.
Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated.
The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.
During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent.
"I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."
In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.
He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator in indirect talks with the US, was similarly dismissive of the CNN report.
"Same false flags, same war mongering, new logos," he posted on X.
Mick Mulroy, a former CIA paramilitary officer and deputy assistant defence secretary, told the BBC: "A dirty bomb is not difficult to make or deploy."
"Although it is not a weapon of mass destruction, it can be a weapon of mass disruption," he added.
Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb.
"But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now."
It comes as intelligence officials and members of the Trump administration seek congressional renewal of a key national security law.
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), which allows the US to spy on foreign nationals, expires next March.

A69.text:
BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attack
Russian strikes hit two key bridges in Kyiv, with Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko saying the Ukrainian capital had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies overnight.
Elsewhere, images shared by President Volodymyr Zelensky showed a missile approaching Crimean Bridge. Zelensky said it was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014, the bridge was personally opened by Putin in 2018.
The BBC's Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Sarah Rainsford, has this report from one of the bridges hit by Russia in Kyiv.

A76.text:
World
Theft of trade, tech secrets 'a global issue' extending beyond recent headlines: security CEO
Recent episodes illustrate risks companies face from those motivated to steal their secrets
Some of the leading tech companies in the U.S. have been finding out recently that the threat of espionage extends into the corporate realm.
At Nvidia, an alleged Chinese spy had a relationship with the company's top executive, Jensen Huang. The scandal has rocked markets, raised national security concerns and led to Huang's ouster. China has denied trying to entrap him. Congress still has questions.
At OpenAI, a former employee was criminally charged after allegedly planting a listening device in a conference room. FBI Director Kash Patel has said that was done "to secretly capture sensitive communications" about the company's technology. The accused has pleaded not guilty to illegally intercepting communications.
And at Google, a former employee was charged and accused of stealing AI technology from the company. In January, a jury convicted the man of multiple counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets — with prosecutors stating the theft had benefitted China. A judge later dismissed the espionage-related counts.
These episodes have shone a light on the ongoing threat to companies — and by extension, the wider economy — from efforts to surreptitiously steal information and secrets. These include efforts involving state or state-linked actors.
In Canada, authorities warn that the risks of these types of actions are increasing at a time when the global economy is becoming more competitive and some of the country's key sectors hold knowledge and insights of interest to hostile actors.
A man walks past an OpenAI booth at a tech summit in San Francisco in September. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)
Yet the drive to steal secrets extends beyond the AI and tech sectors — and beyond borders, warns Don Aviv, the CEO of security firm Interfor International.
"This is a global issue," Aviv told CBC News in an interview.
These events happen when a secret can be surreptitiously obtained that will benefit another party, he said.
A problem for Canada, too
Canada's national intelligence agency, CSIS, has warned that the country is "a target" for states seeking "to acquire sensitive research and technology to advance their own strategic political, economic and military advantage."
In its 2025 public report, the spy agency predicted these threats will increase amid a more competitive global economy, as states jostle for advantages.
AI is one area of interest for states to target at the moment, but it's not the only one that has their attention, according to Stephanie Carvin, an associate professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Affairs at Carleton University in Ottawa.
"It's not just about AI, it's a whole range of high-level technologies," Carvin, a former national security analyst for CSIS, told CBC Radio's Fresh Air.
"In any kind of high-tech area, which is considered to be a strategic priority, where intellectual property is valuable — these are going to be targets as well," she added.
Ottawa has made defending the economy a top priority of its new national security strategy.
The framework plan says "Canadian workers, firms, and innovators need a secure foundation, free from foreign interference, espionage and economic predation, so their efforts can build a prosperous future for all Canadians."
One measure Ottawa plans to take, according to the strategy, is to strengthen the sharing of intelligence information with the private sector and with research institutions. The government says it will also "build intelligence, counterintelligence and security screening capacity to support these partnerships."
Defending against threats
There are companies, like Aviv's own, which provide training on how to prevent these incidents and defend against them.
[truncated]

A79.text:
World
Multiple tech outages have Americans asking: Can somebody fix this?
Officials from FAA, Microsoft, U.S. banks, National Security Agency blame technical glitches
First, Microsoft platforms went down.
Next, thousands of flights were grounded across the U.S. over an air traffic control communications outage.
Then, customers of three major U.S. banks couldn't use their accounts online and United Airlines reported a widespread problem with its system for managing flight departures.
The latest? The classified internal communications network of the National Security Agency — whose mandate includes protecting government communications networks — went offline on Tuesday.
In all cases, officials are blaming the outages on technical glitches, saying there's no evidence of cyberattacks.
Asked Tuesday by a reporter if he's concerned about the outages, U.S. President Donald Trump brushed off the question.
"No, it's life," Trump said at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Manila. "When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no suggestion the outage events were related to one another or to some kind of opponent.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," he said Tuesday.
Despite Trump's reassurance that everything's fine, there are plenty of Americans asking what the heck is going on, including experts like Michael Allen, who served as special assistant for national security to former president George W. Bush.
The successive outages are "a bit fishy," Allen, who is managing director of Beacon Global Strategies, a Washington D.C. firm that advises companies on national security issues, told CNN on Tuesday.
"It really makes me wonder how secure United States infrastructure is, especially in an age of artificial intelligence when it's much easier to be able to find vulnerabilities inside of computer networks than it used to be."
'These developments are troubling'
In Washington, the top Democrat in the U.S. House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, also has questions.
"These developments are troubling and it's unclear if it's all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity," Jeffries told reporters on Capitol Hill Tuesday.
"I think it's time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken."
Jeffries said he's particularly interested in finding out more about what triggered the Federal Aviation Administration to order Friday's nationwide ground stop of flights.
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic Party's leader in the U.S. House of Representatives, arrives for a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)
"There are still more questions than answers in terms of what happened, why it happened, how do we prevent it from happening again," Jeffries said.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has pinned the blame on a newly installed router overloading the national air traffic control's communication system, causing intermittent gaps in radar coverage and communication with pilots.
Duffy promises answers on router
"The root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity as of yet," Duffy told reporters on Capitol Hill Tuesday.
"When I know what happened with that router, injecting that overload into our system, I will most definitely share that with you," he said.
[truncated]

A96.text:
Estados Unidos bombardeó la isla iraní de Qeshm, en el estrecho de Ormuz, horas después de que Teherán atacara Baréin por tercera vez en cinco días.
Un funcionario militar estadounidense le dijo a AFP que cazas "utilizaron munición de precisión para atacar en defensa propia una base de lanzamiento de misiles del Cuerpo de la Guardia Revolucionaria Islámica (CGRI) en la isla de Qeshm".
La fuente añadió que el ataque se produjo en respuesta a una "agresión iraní dirigida contra personal y activos estadounidenses".
La agencia de prensa oficial de Irán había reportado antes "cinco o seis explosiones" en Qeshm este martes, sin causar daños, según el vicegobernador provincial.
Todos los ataques contra Baréin fueron interceptados, incluido el de este martes, según las autoridades bareiníes.
Baréin es uno de los países del Golfo que ha sufrido numerosos ataques de Teherán desde el inicio de la guerra en Medio Oriente, desencadenada por los bombardeos estadounidenses e israelíes contra Irán el 28 de febrero.
El reino concentra numerosos objetivos estratégicos y alberga una de las principales bases navales estadounidenses del mundo, lo que lo convierte en el país "más vulnerable a los ataques", explicó Andreas Krieg, analista del King's College de Londres.
Esta tarde, el Estado Mayor de las Fuerzas Armadas de Kuwait confirmó que estaban respondiendo a un ataque enemigo con drones - aunque no identificó de qué país eran- e informó "cualquier explosión que se pueda escuchar es el resultado de la interceptación de objetivos hostiles por parte de los sistemas de defensa aérea".
Repunte de las hostilidades
Más temprano, Irán reivindicó un nuevo ataque contra una base estadounidense en Baréin, el tercero en cinco días, lo que supone un repunte de las hostilidades dentro de la guerra en Medio Oriente, que se había calmado relativamente desde septiembre.
El CGRI indicó que habían atacado con drones de combate "un sistema de radar operado por fuerzas estadounidenses" en la base aérea de Sheikh Isa, como respuesta a las "repetidas violaciones del espacio aéreo iraní por parte de drones del ejército estadounidense", informó Sepah News.
Los combates entre Estados Unidos e Irán están en pausa desde septiembre, pero el viernes y el domingo los Guardianes reivindicaron ataques contra sistemas estadounidenses de radar en Baréin.
El ejército estadounidense aseguró que derribó los dos drones lanzados por las fuerzas iraníes ese día, y las fuerzas armadas de Baréin indicaron que interceptaron el ataque del domingo.
Ataques químicos
Y una información divulgada por la prensa estadounidense, según la cual Teherán estaría preparando, según CNN, un ataque químico contra Washington atizó la tensión.
"En las últimas 72 horas, los medios proisraelíes 'informaron' que Irán estaría tramando utilizar armas químicas en Washington, construyendo bases militares bajo represas", declaró el ministro de Relaciones Exteriores iraní, Abás Araqchi, en X. "Ahórrennos esta propaganda (...) nadie se la cree", apuntó.
En cambio, el presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump, respondió a una periodista que él se toma "muy en serio" la posibilidad de ese ataque.
Llamado a la moderación
Qatar, mediador clave en el conflicto, hizo un llamado a la moderación y advirtió sobre el riesgo de una escalada.
En este contexto de tensión, el ejército estadounidense había anunciado la víspera que un tercer portaaviones ya estaba operativo en Medio Oriente.
La guerra figurará previsiblemente entre los principales temas de una cumbre tripartita que se celebrará esta semana en China entre Trump y sus homólogos chino, Xi Jinping, y ruso, Vladimir Putin.

The back-and-forth attacks were a reminder of the hurdles facing diplomatic efforts to end a war that has destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and helped fuel the US voter anger that punished President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the November elections.
The Iranian army said it had targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base, after the US ally said its air defences were countering hostile drone attacks. It was the first Iranian attack on the oil-rich country since September.
Neighbouring Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks for the third time this week. It accused Tehran of maintaining a "systematic hostile approach" of targeting the country, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen said it destroyed a cruise missile launched by the militia towards the Saudi capital of Riyadh.
On Tuesday, on the opposite side of the Gulf, US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island, said a US military official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The official said the strike was in response to Iran's attacks on US personnel and assets.
Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure.
THREAT AGAINST WASHINGTON
Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack on Washington, when asked about a CNN report that cited US intelligence assessments on a potential Iranian plot involving a so-called dirty bomb.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital.
Iran's Foreign Ministry had denied the allegations on Tuesday, calling them "baseless."
A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to disperse radioactive material. Unlike a nuclear weapon, it does not produce a nuclear explosion, but can spread radioactive contamination and cause significant disruption and public alarm.
There are diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict, which started when the US and Israel struck Iran on February 28 and has since widened to include Iranian strikes on Israel and US assets in the Middle East.
Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said.
That followed a visit to Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi, where he held talks on safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, Oman's Foreign Ministry said.
SHIPPING DISRUPTED
Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global energy supplies before the war but which is now partly blocked by Iran.
Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war.
Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
A surge in tanker attacks since October threatens to further strain global oil supplies. On Tuesday, a crew abandoned a liquefied petroleum gas tanker off Oman's Khasab.
Meanwhile, Iran has kept pressure on Washington through its Houthi allies, who have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia — the world's largest oil exporter — while tightening control over Yemen's Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opposite Hormuz, in an effort to squeeze Gulf oil producers.
(Reporting by Enas Alashray in Cairo; Writing by Nayera Abdallah, Editing by Sanjeev Miglani, Edwina Gibbs , Stephen Coates and John Mair)

By Raphael Satter, Trevor Hunnicutt, Nandita Bose and Bo Erickson
The NSA said its network experienced a "temporary degradation" during routine maintenance, but that "mission-critical capabilities" remained operational. The series of disruptions to critical systems, which also touched the banking system on Monday, prompted even some Trump allies to demand more information.
"If this is all a coincidence, it's like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world," US Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, told reporters.
Trump earlier played down the incidents, which raised questions of whether the government and private sector had moved too quickly in cutting tech staff.
"It's like when you're big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It's fine," Trump told reporters in Manila, where he was attending meetings with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who doubles as national security adviser, acknowledged the incidents were "unsettling" but said they were completely unrelated.
"We are not under systemic attack," he told reporters in Manila.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyberhackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio added.
DAILY DOWNTIME
Technology-related disruptions have hit every weekday since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.
The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop that lasted 4-1/2 hours, the longest halt to US air travel since the attacks of September 11, 2001.
The spate of outages included a United AirlinesUAL.O technology failure on Monday that delayed about 150 flights on the same day that a JPMorgan ChaseJPM.N software problem disrupted some banking services.
On Tuesday, Apple AAPL.O said it was working to restore its systems after an internal update caused an outage that affected customer services including iCloud and Apple Pay. The issue was not caused by a cyberattack, Apple said.
Insurance provider Marsh MRSH.N also said on Tuesday its clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October — more than double the 48 recorded in the final two weeks of May.
Experts worry that AI tools are feeding a surge of cyberactivity, with cybersecurity companies regularly turning up examples of hackers using AI to launch scores of intrusions at once.
"The recent string of major disruptions across industries highlights how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software update can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems," said Cynthia Kaiser, a former senior FBI cyber official and current senior vice president of cybersecurity firm Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center.
The string of tech outages is likely due to issues emerging from system upgrades, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in an interview with Fox Business on Tuesday.
"We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack ... And we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here. And we can be fairly confident in that," Clayton said.
He attributed the NSA outage to patches deployed for a PHP vulnerability discovered using AI last month — a bug that could let hackers remotely take control of servers.
"Everybody recognizes it's time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they're not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected," Clayton told the "Claman Countdown" program on Fox Business.
OUTAGES FOLLOW LAYOFFS, WARNINGS
At many organizations — both private and government — the outages follow layoffs and, in some cases, explicit warnings about potential disruptions.

Nach Angriff auf Kertschbrücke Selenskyj sieht Ukraine bei Waffenentwicklung als Nummer eins in Europa
Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj sieht im Angriff auf die für Russland strategisch wichtige Kertschbrücke einen Nachweis der eigenen Stärke. Die dafür eingesetzten Drohnen und Marschflugkörper hätten eine gute Trefferquote und hätten sich bewährt, schrieb er am späten Abend auf der Plattform X. »All dies sind Waffen aus ukrainischer Produktion.« Bei der Technologieentwicklung im Verteidigungssektor gehöre die Ukraine derzeit weltweit zu den Top Drei. »In Europa sind wir meiner Meinung nach die Nummer eins.«
Selenskyj sagte weiter, die Technologien und Unternehmen seines Landes entwickelten sich sehr gut. »Wir haben auf russische Angriffe reagiert und werden dies auch weiterhin tun. Wir dürfen vor den Russen nicht zurückschrecken.«
Beschädigte Kertschbrücke
Foto:
Ukrainian Security Service / AFP
In der Nacht zu Dienstag hatte das ukrainische Militär die Brücke vom russischen Festland auf die Halbinsel Krim mit einem massiven Luftangriff teilweise zerstört. Für die Ukrainer ist es einer der bedeutendsten Erfolge in dem seit fast fünf Jahren andauernden Krieg gegen die russischen Invasoren.
Die Brücke über die Meerenge von Kertsch gilt als Prestigeprojekt von Kremlchef Wladimir Putin. Mit 19 Kilometer Länge schuf sie die erste feste Verbindung vom russischen Festland auf die Krim. Über die Brücke versorgte Russland auch seine Truppen auf der Krim und in der besetzten Südukraine.
Pistorius kontert US-Kritik
Bundesverteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius hat unterdessen die Kritik der US-Regierung an ukrainischen Angriffen auf russische Ziele weit abseits der Frontlinien scharf zurückgewiesen. »Angriffe dieser Art in Russland zu kritisieren, mit denen strategische militärische Ziele und militärisch genutzte Einrichtungen zerstört werden sollen, ist meiner Meinung nach ziemlich dumm«, sagte Pistorius auf Englisch nach einem Treffen von Verbündeten der Ukraine im Nato-Hauptquartier in Brüssel.
Statt solche Angriffe zu kritisieren, sollte man vielmehr über die terroristischen Angriffe sprechen, die Tag und Nacht auf die zivile Energie- und Wasserversorgung sowie die Heizungsinfrastruktur in der Ukraine verübt würden. »Das ist eine Form von Terrorismus. Und darüber sollten wir sprechen, statt über rechtmäßige und legitime Angriffe auf nicht zivile Ziele in Russland«, sagte der SPD-Politiker.
Seitens der USA hatte es nach der teilweisen Zerstörung der Krimbrücke durch die ukrainische Armee deutliche Kritik an der Zielauswahl der Militärführung gegeben. »Während sich die öffentliche Debatte auf die spektakulären Angriffe weit hinter den Frontlinien konzentriert, die darauf abzielen, der russischen Bevölkerung Leid zuzufügen, kommen wir zu der Einschätzung, dass solche Angriffe weder dazu beigetragen haben, ein Ende des Krieges herbeizuführen, noch dazu, den russischen Vormarsch an der Front aufzuhalten«, sagte Verteidigungsstaatssekretär Elbridge Colby bei dem Treffen der sogenannten Ukrainekontaktgruppe.

A143.text:
Vertrauter von Eisenkot Israelische Opposition übernimmt Parlamentsvorsitz
Der Parlamentsvorsitz im israelischen Knesset wechselt in die Opposition: Drei Wochen nach der Parlamentswahl in Israel ist der Opposition mit der Wahl eines neuen Parlamentspräsidenten aus den eigenen Reihen ein wichtiger Schritt nach vorn gelungen. 66 von 120 Abgeordneten stimmten für den früheren Minister Matan Kahana. Der 54-Jährige gehört der Mitte-Partei Jaschar an, deren Vorsitzender Gadi Eisenkot derzeit mit der Bildung einer neuen Regierung beauftragt ist.
Kahana löst Amir Ohana ab, der der rechtskonservativen Likud-Partei des bisherigen Ministerpräsidenten Benjamin Netanyahu angehört. Das Oppositionslager erhofft sich von dem Wechsel mehr Einfluss auf die parlamentarischen Abläufe. Ziel ist es, zentrale Elemente des umstrittenen Justizumbaus rückgängig zu machen, den Netanyahus Regierung seit Anfang 2023 vorangetrieben hat.
Der rechtsextreme Finanzminister Bezalel Smotrich hatte Kahana zuvor davor gewarnt, das Amt mit den »Stimmen der Feinde Israels« anzutreten. Damit spielte er auf die arabischen Parteien an. Kahana forderte Smotrich seinerseits auf, den demokratischen Prozess und dessen Ergebnisse zu respektieren. Die arabischen Parteien stimmten wie erwartet für Kahana. Einige Abgeordnete des Lagers von Netanyahu reagierten darauf mit »Schande«-Rufen.
Netanyahus Likud-Partei schickte derweil den Abgeordneten Ofir Katz als Kandidaten für das Amt des Parlamentspräsidenten ins Rennen. Dieser erhielt aber nicht genügend Stimmen.
Kahana diente zunächst in der Eliteeinheit Sajeret Matkal und war anschließend 24 Jahre lang Pilot bei der israelischen Luftwaffe, zuletzt im Rang eines Obersts. Der ausgebildete Jurist setzt sich für eine Stärkung der jüdischen Identität Israels ein, plädiert in Religionsfragen aber für mehr Kompromissbereitschaft und weniger Einfluss der ultraorthodoxen Parteien.
Die Parlamentswahl vom 27. Oktober brachte weder Netanyahus rechtsreligiösem Lager noch dem von Gadi Eisenkot angeführten Oppositionslager eine Mehrheit. Präsident Isaac Herzog beauftragte den früheren Generalstabschef Eisenkot mit der Regierungsbildung. Dafür hat er zunächst bis zum 6. Dezember Zeit, mit einer möglichen Verlängerung um 14 Tage.
Ob es ihm gelingt, eine Koalition zustande zu bringen, ist aber noch offen. Zwischen und innerhalb der politischen Lager gibt es erhebliche Konflikte und zahlreiche rote Linien, die Kompromisse erschweren. Dazu zählt auch die Frage einer möglichen Zusammenarbeit mit arabischen oder streng religiösen Parteien.

Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington
November 17, 2026
Iran on Tuesday dismissed a CNN report that Tehran was preparing a so-called "dirty bomb plot."
US President Donald Trump said his administration was taking the report "very seriously."
What did reports say about an Iranian attack on Washington?
Tehran's dismissal came after CNN reported on Tuesday that "Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC," citing multiple US intelligence sources.
The article also reported that "US intelligence has picked up Iranian chatter claiming that it has stashed bomb-making materials inside the country" and that "many national security officials assume that pre-positioned nuclear materials have already been in the US for years," citing, again, multiple US intelligence sources.
When asked about the story during his visit to the Philippines, Trump said that if there was such a threat, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.
Iran decries 'fabrication'
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei slammed the report, calling it "a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda."
"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations," he said on X.
"Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," he said, naming CNN's reporting on the alleged "dirty bomb plot" and The New York Times without specifying any of its reporting.
Baghaei also said the US and Israel hit water storage reservoirs "during the recent acts of aggression."
Where does the Iran war stand?
The Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, continues as negotiations to bring an end to the fighting stall.
Both US and Israel have been holding off from major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.
Tehran has said it is in control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway. There are near-daily reports of ships hitting mines in parts of the strait Tehran says are unauthorized for transit.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait.
Before the midterm elections, Trump said, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes that started the war, though he did not provide any timeframe.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of an APEC leaders' summit in China on Thursday and discuss ending the war in Iran.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.
Qatar, another mediator in the war, on Tuesday called for restraint "to avoid any escalation that could undermine negotiation efforts."

The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The newly-elected speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu. Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched some seven hours.
In his first comments as speaker, Kahana struck a conciliatory note. “It is possible to be divided and hold opposing positions, yet still respect the institutions of the state and, above all, respect those who think differently,” he said. “The Knesset of Israel is the home of all the citizens of the state of Israel, and I intend to be the speaker of everyone.”
The vote took place weeks after Oct. 27 parliamentary elections in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently given the task by Israel’s president to try to form a new coalition government.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of Tuesday’s vote.
Israel’s final election results give neither Netanyahu nor the opposition a majority
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition. As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with the Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly-sworn in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda. They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks and to reverse laws to limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira with the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Currently a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, Roy Folkman, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would likely give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone,” Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed.”
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee, and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.

Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the vital Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, calling it an “unprecedented” operation as Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day.

Eisenkot-led bloc replaces Netanyahu ally as Parliament speaker
- Israel’s Parliament chose Matan Kahana as speaker, replacing Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana. The vote gives the Eisenkot-led bloc more control over legislation.

JERUSALEM – Israel’s parliament voted on Nov 17 to select a new speaker opposed to the agenda of Benjamin Netanyahu, a potential first step in rolling back the prime minister’s divisive political agenda even as his main rival struggles to form a government.
Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party, with 66 voting in favor of Kahana and 52 voting for another candidate, according to the office of the spokesperson for the Parliament.
Kahana replaces Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party.
“The Knesset of Israel is the home of all citizens of the State of Israel, and I intend to be the Speaker for everyone,” said Kahana in his inaugural speech.
In Israel’s unicameral 120-seat Parliament, known as the Knesset, the speakership is a powerful position that wields considerable influence, including over what legislation is brought to a vote.
Kahana will have the ability to advance bills prioritised by the Eisenkot-led bloc and other parties backing the former general in his bid to become prime minister.
These include establishing an independent inquiry into the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attack, which Netanyahu has opposed; imposing term limits on the prime minister; and repealing laws passed by the previous Netanyahu-led government that critics said curtailed the powers of the judiciary.
Netanyahu’s Likud party condemned the vote, saying lawmakers elected Kahana with “the votes of terror supporters”. Throughout the election campaign, Netanyahu attacked Israel’s Arab-led parties saying that they represent an existential threat to Israel, in attacks that the parties condemned as racist and discriminatory.
Members of the Eisenkot-led bloc have also been appointed to chair several key parliamentary committees, which play an important role in advancing legislation.
The Parliament was sworn in on Nov 10 without a new government, after a deadlocked Oct 27 general election stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left his main rivals with no clear path to power.
Deadlocked election aftermath
President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar political party, with forming a government. However, the former chief of the military also lacks a majority and will likely have to compromise on some campaign promises if he is to secure the support needed to form a government.
Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a government is formed. His right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held in 2027.
Netanyahu has sought to cast doubt on the election results by baselessly alleging voter fraud by Arabs, who make up a fifth of the population. Election officials have said that they are probing potential misconduct but that they have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the vote's outcome.

NEW YORK - Apple is working to restore its systems after an internal update caused wide-scale outages on Nov 17, disrupting the App Store, employee tools, retail operations and consumer services.
The outages are the latest in a string of similar incidents that have occurred recently at US companies and government agencies.
Last week a bug inside of Microsoft Corp’s data centres crippled some of the software giant’s popular tools, including Outlook, Teams and the Copilot assistant.
On Nov 13, flights in the US were grounded for more than four hours after equipment outages affected Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control facilities.
On Nov 16, JPMorgan Chase, the largest US bank, suffered from a “technical issue” that also affected other financial institutions.
And the National Security Agency is suffering an outage of a classified computer network it uses for internal communications and other daily work functions, Bloomberg News reported earlier on Nov 17.
The outages at Apple knocked out several internal services, including AppleWeb, the employee portal, AppleConnect, the internal sign-in system, and virtual private network access for remote workers, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
Employees also had trouble downloading internal software builds, accessing company calendars and booking conference rooms.
Even the internal website that tracks outages went down, said the people, who asked not to be named discussing internal matters.
Many employees were unable to access systems that required their Apple credentials for several hours, leaving them unable to work.
The outages also affected Apple stores around the world, disrupting sales, repairs and customer service.
The problems extended to consumer services, including access to iCloud and the ability to sign up for AppleCare directly on a device, according to Apple’s online status page.
Services for schools and businesses were also affected.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the Cupertino, California-based company said in a statement.

A604.text:
EU proposes €45bn loan to Ukraine to cover two-thirds of its funding gap for 2027
Von der Leyen is now speaking in Brussels.
She says that the EU will engage in any peace talks on ending the war, while ensuring “maximum support” for Ukraine and “maximum pressure” on Russia.
She says Ukraine has a €70bn funding gap for 2027, and the European Commission proposes a €45bn loan to Ukraine to help cover its 2027 financing needs, with €25bn earmarked for military needs, and €20bn for budget support.
“We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiation table, and Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”
The final third of the gap will have to be covered by other external partners, she said.
This proposal will be put to EU leaders at the next summit in two weeks’ time.
EU's von der Leyen insists all EU27 will support loan for Ukraine
The commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is asked which governments will take part in the loan, given that at least four – Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia – have signalled they do not want to be involved.
She strikes a determined tone as she says it’s different from the previous loan (where three countries were given an opt-out) and all countries need to participate as she directly links it with the EU’s budget.

She says that since the loan has two elements – civilian and military – those countries that do not want to provide any funding for Ukraine’s military can still take part in the other part of the loan.
“I’m very confident that we will agree by 27 because, as I said, all 27 member states support Ukraine explicitly.”
Well, let’s see about that.
That ends the press conference – I will bring you any reaction from the four potential breakaway leaders when we get it.

EU’s economy commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis offers a bit of detail on how the loan is supposed to work.

He says the loan could also be repaid through profits on immobilised Russian assets (in a funny slip of tongue, he appears to briefly call them Soviet assets before self-correcting himself to sovereign assets).
Also worth noting that Dombrovski is wearing a Latvian-coloured ribbon in his lapel to mark the Proclamation Day of the Republic of Latvia, the independence day.
EU will pursue 22nd package of sanctions as it 'stands united' in support for Ukraine, von der Leyen says

“Sanctions work. They are not inflicting a sudden blow to the Russian economy, but they erode its foundations. And we have many indicators by now that point to a worsening outlook for the Russian economy and real difficulties.”
She adds the EU’s decisions intend to “send a clear message to Russia.”

A609.text:
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.
The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.
They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.
Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.
